scores.evidence: On Linux and macOS, Python's `os.rename` silently overwrites an existing file.
scores.rationale: Claims about ExifTool coverage, POSIX vs Windows rename semantics, QuickTime UTC storage, Keys:CreationDate offsets, the 32k Windows command-line limit, and case-insensitive filesystem behavior are all accurate and precise, including the subtle areas.

scores.evidence: A custom tool is only worth building for preview, undo, keeping Live Photo and RAW+JPEG pairs together, and safe re-runs.
scores.rationale: Solves exactly the stated problem, resolves ambiguities (dry-run default, skip-vs-guess, timezone) with sensible defaults, excludes scope explicitly with reasons, and even questions whether the tool is needed at all.

scores.evidence: The flow is strictly one-way... `plan` is pure logic with no input/output... `execute` doesn't make decisions.
scores.rationale: Components have single clear responsibilities, data ownership is tabulated, interfaces connect, and the plan/execute/journal/undo decisions are honored consistently in every section with no contradictions.

scores.evidence: For every k, making the k-th `os.rename` fail leaves the folder listing and file hashes identical to the start.
scores.rationale: Fault-injection, property tests, early time-boxed spikes with explicit 'changes the plan if' conditions, a golden corpus of real files, and checkable milestone exit criteria target precisely the plan's riskiest assumptions before commitment.

scores.evidence: A1 | Users are technical and can install ExifTool. | If they aren't... bundle the `.exe` or switch to a pure-Python reader
scores.rationale: Every design-bearing assumption is tabulated with impact-if-wrong and a validation point, numbers are marked as estimates or assumptions, and open questions have stated defaults so work can proceed.

scores.evidence: `photoname undo DIR` uses the identities in the header to find each file, whether it is at its original name, its temp name or its target.
scores.rationale: Covers the hard domain failures — crash mid-run, locked files, bogus EXIF dates, rename chains, case-insensitive and exFAT filesystems, cloud placeholders, untrusted metadata — each with concrete detection, containment and recovery.

scores.evidence: Clear exit codes: 0 success, 1 rolled back, 2 setup or usage error, 3 manual action needed.
scores.rationale: For a single-user CLI the operational story is complete: pipx install/rollback, versioned journal format, structured logs, a troubleshooting README, and burden sized to one part-time developer.

scores.evidence: Cost: none to run. ExifTool and Python are free... Sizes are focused developer-days.
scores.rationale: Correctly identifies that engineering time is the dominant cost, gives labeled per-milestone estimates and a performance estimate marked for measurement, and makes the build-vs-buy trade-off explicit via the one-liner alternative.

scores.evidence: ExifTool behind a `MetadataReader` interface... the interface keeps a pure-Python reader possible later.
scores.rationale: Each decision carries a reversibility rating and revisit trigger; the persisted journal is versioned, the hard-to-reverse name-stability and language choices get scrutiny, and reversible choices are made quickly.

scores.evidence: There is no database... `argparse`... No dependencies, and the journal travels with the folder.
scores.rationale: A single-process tool with the minimal dependency set; the only added machinery (journal, two-phase rename) is justified by irreversibility of original names, and nothing speculative is built.

scores.evidence: Create the repository and do T1: `mkdir photoname && cd photoname && git init`
scores.rationale: Tasks T1–T11 have explicit ordering with dependency reasons, concrete done-when criteria, and spikes state exactly what results would change the plan, so a team could start immediately.

checklist.evidence: For photos: `DateTimeOriginal` (+ subseconds), then `CreateDate`, then skip.
It rejects `0000:00:00` and years before 1990 or in the future... Skip. A `--fallback mtime` flag lets you opt in.
groups with the same base name are sorted by (subsecond, original name). The first gets the base name; the rest get `_01`, `_02`
Dry run is the default. Nothing changes on disk unless you pass `--apply`.
First check that the target doesn't exist (`os.path.lexists`)... running the tool again on a finished folder changes nothing.
Every apply is journaled... `undo` reads the most recent journal. It moves each file back after checking its identity.
Camera clock time is used as recorded. Photos get no timezone conversion... Requests... `OffsetTimeOriginal`
Keep related files under the same base name: Live Photo HEIC+MOV pairs, RAW+JPEG pairs, and `.xmp` / `.aae` sidecar files
default `%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S`... Every target is a single path component with no `/ \ : * ? " < > |`... keeps its own extension

traps.evidence: First check that the target doesn't exist (`os.path.lexists`); on Windows `os.rename` also refuses to overwrite.
For photos: `DateTimeOriginal` (+ subseconds)... mtime fallback only by opt-in
There is no database... Removing duplicates, a GUI, cloud photo libraries... [are non-goals]
Writing or fixing metadata... [is a non-goal]; `scan` does not read file contents.
default `%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S`... No target is a Windows reserved name such as `CON` or `NUL`.

note: An exemplary plan: technically precise on EXIF/filesystem subtleties, safety-first (dry-run default, journaled two-phase renames, undo), proportionate to a small CLI, and immediately actionable; it avoids every trap and concretely addresses every checklist item.
